newsitem.title: USA: Iraq distribution plan submission week-10 days off.
newsitem.headline: Iraq distribution plan submission week-10 days off.

text.p: A senior U.N. humanitarian aid official said on Monday that Iraq remained a week to 10 days away from submitting a finalized distribution aid plan to start the oil sales process for the renewed "oil-for-food" accord.

"Iraq has not completed their plan, the plan for the north (Kurdish regions of Iraq) is not completed. It will be at least one week before it comes to us. We (the U.N.) have people in Baghdad who tell us the plan is not ready," said the U.N. official.

Even though the U.N. Security Council rolled over the oil accord for another 180 days from June 8, there have been no new oil sales or subsequent oil liftings. Before there can be new contracts, Iraq must submit a new distribution plan for U.N. approval, followed by a fresh oil pricing formula.

In recent weeks, Iraqi government officials have tied the submission of such plans to speeding-up aid contract approvals, and the resulting drawing down of some $800 million sitting in a New York-based escrow account deposited from first round oil receipts.
Baghdad blames the U.S. for putting holds on food and medicine contracts, and slowing distribution of supplies to civilians, the intended recipients of oil sales proceeds.
Still, Western diplomats have said they expect oil sales to resume shortly after the Iraqis submit their distribution plan, a time which may come in early to mid-July.

The senior U.N. aid official said a timetable was impossible to forecast, but noted that the amount of time it takes the U.N. to approve a distribution plan depends entirely on the contents of Baghdad's submission.

"Some sectors of the plan can simply be repeated. Some demand the writing out of a new program. If our people participate with the Iraqis along the way, it should take only a few days to approve, but we haven't seen anything yet," said the senior official.

The basics of the distribution plan detail what food and supplies Baghdad wants to buy from oil sales, but new details will be needed for programs to rehabilitate Iraqi water and sewage sectors, and other fundamental infrastructure.

U.N. Security Council stern warnings to Iraq over the weekend of further sanctions if does not abide by allowing unfettered U.N. arms inspections, has no linkage to the "oil-for-food" scheme, U.N. officials stressed.

"The Iraqis have had their problems with UNSCOM (U.N. Special Commission inspectors), a poor record with UNSCOM. But, they cooperate reasonably well, even more than reasonably well with us," said the aid official.

Iraq sealed a deal with the U.N. last year to permit it to sell $2 billion worth of crude oil over a 180-day period, in order to buy food and medicine for civilians suffering from broad sanctions applied after Saddam Hussein's forces invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
The original "oil-for-food" round ran from December 10, 1996 to June 7, and was successful in having Iraq sell its allotted oil quota.
